results.message: What was a sermon like at Hippo?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
A sermon at Hippo was the ordinary work of the man answerable for that flock. Augustine preached to the whole church, baptized or still learning, again and again, the same voice working on the same people. It was not a lecture and not a show. It was the man in charge of them, telling them to his face what he thought they needed. The people were not a silent audience. Possidius tells us that when Augustine came to Hippo as a presbyter, the congregation seized him and loudly told their own bishop to ordain him. Possidius wrote: “The Catholics already knew the life and teaching of the holy Augustine, and they seized him. He was standing there among the people, feeling safe and unaware of what was about to happen... So they seized him and, as is the custom in such cases, brought him to the bishop to be ordained. They did this because all of them, with one accord, wanted it done and carried through. They demanded it with great eagerness and loud shouting, while he wept freely.”

That clamour was the same suffrage that put Cyprian into office, over his own reluctance, a century and a half earlier. The people could demand, and the bishop answered for what he gave them. When they failed it was not a problem he managed but a wound he carried, and when they would not hear him he wept.

glosses.plain_meaning: We are not a silent audience. We put men into office, and we say so out loud. We can stand in front of a bishop's own seat and refuse to go home.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, 'the people' names the congregation when it acts. They consent, they demand, and they elect -- unlike the flock, which is the congregation being cared for.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener may hear either a passive congregation or a modern democratic electorate with formal voting rights. Neither is right. A corporate body whose consent and demand genuinely constitute a call to office, and which can be exerted disruptively, but which holds no procedural mechanism and can still be refused.
false_friend: a passive congregation with no real leverage over its own clergy
a modern democratic electorate, with a formal ballot and a fixed voting procedure

glosses.plain_meaning: Cyprian named two things that put him in office: our suffrage, and God's judgment. A rival group opposed him, but the people chose him anyway.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, suffrage is the voice of the people that puts a man into office. It can go against his own wishes.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener will hear 'suffrage' as the right to vote, and expect a franchise, a ballot, and a procedure. We mean neither. A corporate acclamation that carries real constitutive force, in a community where the man acclaimed is expected to resist and where an organized faction can oppose without stopping it.
false_friend: the right to vote, with an expected franchise, a ballot, and a fixed procedure

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV, independently re-located this session; Doc_01 SS2); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII; Doc_01 SS2); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo (lpc.story.the-psalms-on-the-wall)

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised (Doc_01 SS2; lpc.story.election-of-cyprian); banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258 (lpc.story.the-death-of-cyprian)

confidence.divergence_note: In the vendored English edition of Cyprian the Latin plebs occurs exactly three times, all inside the 19th-century American editor's own introductory and elucidatory prose, none inside Cyprian's own letters. Cyprian's Latin does use it: Hartel's letters carry plebs in running text, 89 whole-word occurrences with notes excluded, and letter 43 is headed CYPRIANVS PLEBI VNIVERSAE S. 'The people' is the English volume's own recurring rendering for the congregation as an acting body. It is a working handle, and whether plebs becomes the world word is not settled.

The vendored Weiskotten scan carries a single OCR artifact inside this quotation -- 'ancf' for 'and' -- reproduced here exactly as the scan gives it (matching this record's own text against the raw file precisely, per this step's own discipline), not silently corrected; modern_rendering gives the plain sense ('they demanded it...') rather than reproducing the artifact.

They did this because all of them, with one accord, wanted it done and carried through. They demanded it with great eagerness and loud shouting, while he wept freely.”

Our claim that this is a cross-phase pattern rests on both bishops' own conduct of the office, not on matching word-counts in each phase (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes, Lexicon_Deployment_Index.md SS6).
